tagline.text: Rizal relics and Filipino masters inside Makati's RCBC Plaza

location.label: Location
location.text: RCBC Plaza, corner of Ayala Avenue and Sen. Gil Puyat Avenue, Makati City

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (indoors; easier to travel in the dry season, December–May)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱200–500 (admission, transport and a light snack)

children.text: The Yuchengco Museum is a private museum that opened in September 2005 in a four-story building beside RCBC Plaza in Makati. It brings together Ambassador Alfonso Yuchengco's collection, a José Rizal exhibit and contemporary art shows under one roof, which makes it an easy add-on to a Makati day.

The Yuchengco Museum stands inside the RCBC Plaza complex, at the corner of Ayala Avenue and Senator Gil Puyat Avenue in the Makati Central Business District (CBD). It opened in September 2005 to display the art and artifacts collected by Ambassador Alfonso T. Yuchengco, a Filipino banker and diplomat, and it occupies a four-story building attached to the headquarters of the Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation (RCBC). The design is reported to involve Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) and W.V. Coscolluela & Associates.

Ambassador Yuchengco was born in Binondo, Manila, in 1923 and died in 2017 at the age of 94. He served as ambassador to Japan (1995–1998) and to China (1986–1988), and is said to have named his bank after José Rizal, the national hero he admired. That is why one of the permanent exhibits on the top floor is "Buhay Rizal," which follows Rizal's life. You can see his diplomas and certificates, letters exchanged with family and friends, portraits and photographs, and items related to the women in his life.

The collection divides into the Yuchengco family story and paintings by Filipino masters. According to visitor accounts, works by names such as Juan Luna, Fernando Amorsolo, Ang Kiukok, Victorio Edades, Vicente Manansala and Botong Francisco have appeared in permanent or special exhibitions. A portrait of Enrique and Maria Yuchengco painted by Botong Francisco has also been featured. Exhibits change often, so if there is a particular work you want to see, check the museum's official website for the current show before you go. For a first visit, we suggest this order: check what is on at the front desk on the ground floor, go up to the permanent exhibits on the fourth floor for Rizal and the Yuchengco family, then work your way down through the third-floor special exhibitions. The Makati CBD is busy with office workers on weekdays, but the museum itself is relatively calm, so it also works as a place to catch your breath between malls. If you bring children, remind them beforehand not to run or shout. Guided talks and curator-led tours may be held on fixed dates, so it is best to ask in advance if you want one.

This is not a large museum that takes up half a day. Even at a relaxed pace, 1.5 to 2 hours is usually enough, so it fits neatly between shopping or meetings in Makati. As an air-conditioned indoor attraction, it is also a good refuge from midday heat or rainy-season showers. Reviews say impressions vary by floor: the Yuchengco family history and the Rizal exhibit are well regarded, while some special exhibitions are a matter of taste. It suits visitors who are interested in art and want an atmosphere different from Manila's other museums.

On the fourth-floor permanent exhibit you follow the life of José Rizal through letters, certificates, photographs and personal items. If you have already visited Rizal Park or the Calamba birthplace, the story connects even more vividly.

blocks.title: The Legacy of Ambassador Alfonso Yuchengco

children.text: The permanent exhibit "The Legacy of Ambassador Alfonso T. Yuchengco" tells the story of the man who founded the museum and his family. It offers a glimpse into modern Philippine business and diplomatic history.
Visitor accounts mention works by Juan Luna, Amorsolo, Ang Kiukok, Manansala and others. What is actually on the walls differs from time to time, so ask at the front desk when you enter.

blocks.title: Botong Francisco's portrait of the Yuchengco couple

children.text: A portrait by Botong Francisco, famous for his large mural-like canvases, has been shown here. It is a rare chance to see a master's portrait work up close.

The third floor has the Alcove Gallery, the Bridgeway Gallery and the Foyer Gallery, where solo shows rotate. In autumn 2026 these included a Jaime de Guzman exhibition and a serial show by Marco Santos.

blocks.title: YSpace event area on the ground floor

children.text: Besides exhibitions, YSpace on the ground floor hosts talks, tastings and workshops. Schedules and fees differ by event, and many require separate registration.

blocks.title: Architecture and location in the city

children.text: It is a modern four-story building in the middle of Makati's towers. Its appeal is a quiet art space among tall office buildings.

Come down to the third floor for the special exhibitions in the Alcove, Bridgeway and Foyer galleries. Tastes vary on special shows, so feel free to linger only over what appeals to you.

Have lunch at a restaurant around RCBC Plaza and Ayala Avenue. Makati has plenty of choices to suit any budget and taste.

The museum is closed on Sundays and public holidays. Plan this route for Monday to Saturday, and check beforehand whether it is closed around holidays.

From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA), the simplest way to the Makati CBD is a taxi or Grab. Travel time varies greatly with traffic, so avoid rush hours.
Tell the driver "RCBC Plaza, Ayala Avenue corner Sen. Gil Puyat Avenue." Saying RCBC Plaza is easier for drivers to understand than the museum's name.
Fares and travel times vary with the time of day and traffic, so check the estimated fare in the app before you ride.
According to the official guide, it is about
8 minutes
on foot from Ayala MRT Station, while another guide says about 5 minutes (5-10 minutes depending on your pace). Using the air-conditioned walkways, if available, helps you avoid heat and rain.
Bus and jeepney routes and stops change often, so check the current route on a map app.
The official website says there is parking at RCBC Plaza. Check parking fees and conditions on site.
The Makati CBD is very congested at rush hour. If you are coming only for the museum, arriving at opening time is much easier.
The Yuchengco Museum is an indoor attraction, so weather barely affects it. The trip to and from Makati can be tiring, though, so schedule your visit for a drier season when getting around is easier.

The museum is in the Makati CBD, so there are many places to stay. Hotels along Ayala Avenue are easy to reach on foot, and the area near Greenbelt and the Ayala Triangle is convenient for shopping and dining. Room rates vary greatly by season and booking site, so check a local booking app.

For meals, you can eat in the food areas of RCBC Plaza and along Ayala Avenue, or at restaurants around Greenbelt. Korean and Japanese restaurants, Filipino home cooking and cafés are all easy to find, so it is simple to match your group's tastes. Lunchtime (12:00–13:00) is crowded with office workers, so try to avoid the peak.

After the museum, you may enjoy a slow walk around the Ayala Triangle Gardens. A rest among the city greenery followed by a café at Greenbelt rounds off a half-day plan naturally. In the evening the streets fill with commuters, so we suggest moving early.
Before you go, check the current exhibitions and any closures on the official website (yuchengcomuseum.org). Special exhibitions change every few weeks.
The museum is closed on Sundays and public holidays. If you are in Makati on a Sunday, plan something else.
You need ID to get the student, PWD or senior discount. Ask on site whether a Korean student ID is accepted.
Admission fees differ between travel sites. Some older reviews list ₱100 or even free entry, so go by the official information.
The galleries can be strongly air-conditioned, so a light jacket is useful.
If you are interested in Rizal, start on the fourth floor. Even if time runs short, you will not miss the core permanent exhibit.
Photography rules may differ by exhibition, so ask the staff when you enter.
You can make inquiries at +63 2 8889 1234 or info@yuchengcomuseum.org.
The museum is closed on Sundays and public holidays, and its hours and fees may change, so check the official information before you go.
Rush-hour traffic in the Makati CBD is heavy. Allow plenty of travel time.
Fees and exhibitions change often. The information here is as of autumn 2026, so check the latest announcements.
Special exhibitions end quickly, so check the dates if there is a show you want to see.
Be careful of pickpockets and phone snatchers in the city, and it is safer to book taxis through an app.
The museum is not large, so fit it into a Makati itinerary rather than making it the main destination of your day.
A short taxi ride from the museum, this is a mixed-use commercial district for shopping, dining and strolling.
The Philippines' central business district, packed with finance towers, shopping malls and restaurants. It is a nice way to enjoy the city atmosphere after the museum.
See paintings by masters such as Juan Luna, plus natural history and anthropology exhibits. From Makati you can get there by taxi or Grab, and the time depends on traffic.
Manila's best-known park, home to the José Rizal monument, pairs well with the museum's Rizal exhibit.
A modern new downtown that is easy to continue to from Makati. It has plenty of street sculptures and cafés.
